title: Testing your design
objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to plan a fair test that changes one variable at a time, record results clearly, and use them to improve a design.

sections.title: What is a fair test?
sections.text: A fair test treats everything you are comparing in the same way. To find which paper plane flies farthest, throw each one from the same spot, in the same way. If the throws are different, you cannot tell whether the plane or the throw made the difference.

sections.title: Change one thing at a time
sections.text: A variable is anything that can change in a test. Change only one variable, and keep all the others the same. To test which soil helps bean plants grow best, change only the soil, and give every plant the same seeds, water and sunlight.

sections.title: Record your results
sections.text: Write each result in a table straight away, with its unit, such as metres or seconds. Repeat each test at least three times and take the average, just as you did when measuring. A clear record lets you, and others, check your work.

sections.title: Improve and test again
sections.text: Look at your results to find the weak point in your design. Change it, then test again in exactly the same way so you can compare. Engineers go round this loop many times, and a failed test is useful information, not a disaster.

diagram.title: Running a fair test
steps: Repeat the test and record the results
Compare averages and improve the design

check_questions.prompt: Zainab wants to know which of her paper plane designs flies farthest. Which plan is best?
options: Throw each plane in a different way
Throw every plane from the same spot, in the same way
Measure some flights in metres and some in footsteps
check_questions.explanation: Keeping the throw the same means any difference in distance comes from the plane design.

misconception.0: If the throws differ, you cannot tell whether the plane or the throw caused the result.
misconception.2: You need to test every design to compare them.
misconception.3: Mixing units makes the results impossible to compare.

check_questions.prompt: You want to find out which soil helps bean plants grow tallest. Which plan is a fair test?
options: Use different soils, but the same seeds, water and sunlight
Use different soils and give each plant a different amount of water
Use the same soil for every plant
Use different soils and put some plants in the dark
check_questions.explanation: Only the soil changes, so any difference in growth can be put down to the soil.

misconception.1: Two things change at once, so you cannot tell whether the soil or the water made the difference.
misconception.2: If the soil never changes, you learn nothing about which soil is best.
misconception.3: Light also changes, so the test is not fair.

check_questions.prompt: Why should you repeat each test and record every result?
options: Because the first result is always wrong
So you can change several variables at once
So one unusual result does not mislead you
check_questions.explanation: Repeating and averaging means one odd result has less effect, and the record lets you check it.

misconception.0: The point is reliable results, not a longer table.
misconception.1: The first result is not always wrong. Any single result might be unusual.
misconception.2: A fair test changes only one variable at a time.

try_it.title: Try It Yourself
try_it.instructions: Change the three distances to results from your own paper plane test, in metres. Run the code to find the average.
